  * Transparently publish all documentation related to the operation of the "Pulse" club from its opening until the accident from different government and local official institutions.

  * Disciplinary, criminal, and/or political liability of all institutions that are found to have failed in their work related to the incident

  * The Independent Catering Association should start working on improving the services and operating conditions of catering facilities, and not just for deregulation and financial assistance from the state.

* Including those, in an official statement put out by the Liberal Democratic Youth (LiDeM) in North Macedonia also calls demands for:

  * A national anti-corruption initiative focusing on local governance, ensuring that municipal authorities are held responsible for the enforcement of safety laws.

  * Creation of a "Park of Corruption" on the site of the nightclub—an enduring reminder of the price we pay when corruption and negligence go unchecked. This will not only serve as a memorial but as a call to action, urging future generations to fight against a culture that prioritizes profit over human lives.

* The European Commission is to put pressure on the Government of North Macedonia to fulfill all the people’s demands

* The European Commission and European Council to ensure that all of the countries seeking membership in the European Union have the highest level of respect for individual freedoms and human rights, ensure full protection of the right to protest in line with EU standards, and ensure transparent, accountable governance in line with European democratic principles.

  78. ##  **Defending Democracy in Türkiye: Condemning the Arrest of Ekrem Imamoğlu and Political Repression against the Opposition and Civil Society**

(Passed Spring 2025\)

Movers: Bundesverband Liberaler Hochschulgruppen (LHG)

Co-signers: Joventut Nacionalista de Catalunya, Svensk Ungdom, Jovenes Ciudadanos, Radikal Ungdom, JUNOS, Young Progressive Slovakia, Young Liberals, Liberal Youth of Sweden (LUF), Momentum TizenX, Lithuanian Liberal Youth, Unge Venstre, Ze\!Molodizhka, Jeunes MR, Fédération des Etudiants Libéraux (FEL), Nowoczesna Youth, Alliance Youth, Silvia Fernández (IMS), Jonge Democraten, Jongdemocraten, For Youth\!, Centerstudenter, JOVD, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz, LiDem, Jonk Demokraten, Youth Forum Nasa Stranka

*Noting that:*

* In the early morning hours of March 19th 2025, Istanbul’s ruling mayor and leading opposition politician Ekrem Imamoğlu was arrested on charges of corruption and terrorism, along with more than 80 of his close allies.

* The previous day, on March 18th 2025, Istanbul University had suddenly annulled Imamoğlu’s diploma, thereby effectively inhibiting him from contending presidential elections under Turkish law

* Following Imamoğlu’s arrest, Turkish authorities implemented several measures to restrict the public expression of dissent, including a prohibition of any public gatherings, the closure of public squares, the disruption of key transportation routes such as major roads and metro lines, the reduction of internet bandwidth, and restrictions of access to social media  
* Despite the ban on public gatherings, hundreds of thousands Turkish citizens took to the streets all over the country in the largest anti-government protests in over a decade, demanding Imamoğlu’s release and calling for the resignation of the government, including President Erdoğan  
* Turkish riot police brutally cracked down on the protests using tear gas and rubber bullets, and detained nearly 2000 protesters, most of whom were university students  
* Numerous journalists reporting about the protests have either been arrested or deported by Turkish authorities  
* On March 23rd, the same day that he was officially elected and nominated as presidential candidate by his party, a judge ordered Imamoğlu to be transferred to prison pending trial and he was dismissed as mayor of Istanbul

*Considering that:*

* The conspicuous timing of Imamoğlu’s arrest, just 4 days before he was due to be nominated as presidential candidate by the opposition party CHP, strongly suggests a political motive behind the charges against him

* Fifteen million Turkish citizens expressed their solidarity and support for Imamoğlu by voting for him in CHP's primary elections and nominating him as their presidential candidate  
* Imamoğlu is Türkiye’s leading opposition figure and is widely considered to be the only candidate capable of successfully challenging Erdoğan in presidential elections  
* Imamoğlu's arrest follows a common pattern of judicial harassment against opposition politicians, journalists, and civil society actors in Türkiye in recent years  
* The protests arose at a time of widespread dissatisfaction in Turkish society, driven by persistent inflation, soaring living costs, the erosion of democratic institutions, restricted press freedom, and the government’s failure to effectively address these issues

*Believing that:*

* The freedom from arbitrary detention, the freedom of the press, the freedom of association, and the right to fair trial are not only cherished liberal values, but also essential human rights

* Upholding the rule of law is a prerequisite for safeguarding human rights and political freedoms

* A strong and independent opposition is the backbone of any functioning democracy, and consequently, the arbitrary detention of opposition leaders constitutes a grave attack on democratic principles

* The Turkish citizens have the right to freely express their political will, protest peacefully, and participate in fair and transparent elections without fear of repression

*Notwithstanding that:*

Türkiye has proven to be a vital partner for the EU and its member states in areas such as NATO security cooperation, migration and refugee management, conflict resolution and mediation in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as efforts to rebuild Syria, among other issues.  
LYMEC calls for:

* The Turkish government to uphold the rule of law, restore judicial independence, and respect the fundamental rights of opposition figures, journalists, and civil society actors

* The Turkish authorities to release Imamoğlu and his allies with immediate effect and grant them a fair trial under the rule of law

* A continued and escalated pressure on the EU and its member states to strongly condemn the recent developments in Türkiye and make clear that these oppressive measures are incompatible with democratic values and European partnership  
* A continued and escalated pressure on the EU and its members states to formally terminate Türkiye’s stalled EU accession procedure on the grounds of severe violations of democratic principles, human rights, and the rule of law, while explicitly leaving the door open for renewed accession negotiations in a post-Erdoğan era

  81. ## **Cold front: A new era of security in the Arctic**

### ***Passed Autumn 2025***

Submitted by: Norges Unge Venstre (NUV), Junge Liberale (JuLis), Svensk Ungdom (SU)

Co-signed by: Radikal Ungdom (RU), Venstres Ungdom, Young Liberals UK, LLY, LHG, JOVD, Alliance Youth, Nowoczesna Youth

Noting that:

* The Arctic, which has long been characterised by security policy stability with a historically low risk of escalation, has seen a greater power competition over

  the last years.

* Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,, and its growing strategic interest in Arctic resources and routes have shifted it in many Western perceptions from partner to challenger.

* Instances of uncertainty in U.S. foreign policy (e.g. threats over Greenland) have strained trust in alliances and emphasised European dependence on U.S.  
  security guarantees.

* Several European NATO members, especially those in or near the Arctic, have increased concern over Russian military buildup and ambitions in the High North.

* In late September 2025, unauthorised suspected Russian drone activity was observed near multiple airports in Denmark and Norway, causing major disruptions

  and was a reminder of Russian presence in the north.

Emphasising that:

* The security environment in Europe, especially due to Russia’s behavior, demands

  stronger collective defence capabilities and clearer responsibilities among NATO

  members.

* In recent years, Russia has demonstrated an increasing interest in exploiting the many opportunities in the Arctic, such as oil, natural gas, and potential future shipping routes made accessible by climate change.  
* Russia’s ongoing construction of a new military base on Wrangel Island demonstrates its increasing militarisation and strategic interest in the Arctic, with potential implications for NATO operations, environmental protection, and

  the stability of the region.

* Existing frameworks such as the Nordic Defence Cooperation (NORDEFCO) already

  provide a strong foundation for enhancing regional coordination, interoperability, and preparedness in the Arctic region.

* Legal norms and international order (treaties, maritime law, freedom of navigation) are fundamental to stability in the Arctic and must be defended

  accordingly.

* European NATO members have the capacity and interest to take greater ownership  
  of defence in the High North, reducing over-reliance on U.S. presence, but this  
  requires planning, coordination, capability investment, and credible command

  structures.

* The current geopolitical situation in Europe necessitates more proactive European NATO members, ensuring the alliance's interests while preventing Russia’s protectionist developments in the region.

* Nearly all members of the Arctic Council, except Russia, are NATO members, and  
  the risk of escalation does not appear to outweigh the dangers of lacking a presence in the region.

Believing that:

* To protect Europe’s broad range of interests, the Arctic must remain a peaceful

and stable region based on international cooperation and respect for legal principles.

* While seeking collaboration, European countries in NATO must secure adequate

  defence capabilities and preparedness to ensure sovereignty and security in the

  northern areas.

* Arctic security must also be a top priority within the EU defence cooperation and NORDEFCO. Whereas the EU’s role in security policy has sparked debate in

  countries like Denmark, which lifted its defence opt-out in European cooperation, the debate has been largely absent in Norway, despite the fact that

  modern security also encompasses non-military dimensions such as cyber defence,

  energy resilience, disinformation, and supply chain security.

LYMEC calls for:

1. Uphold of International Legal Order

   * Maintain strict adherence to UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the

   Sea) and other binding international treaties relevant to Arctic sovereignty, navigation, and maritime boundaries.

   * Oppose unilateral changes to recognised boundaries or restrictions of navigation

   routes without a legal basis.

   * Support adjudication / legal mechanisms for overlapping sovereignty claims.

   * Prevent Russia from violating international commitments regarding freedom of

   navigation through the Northwest Passage and the Northeast Passage.

2. Strengthened Arctic Defence Posture among European NATO Members

   * Increase investment in military capabilities suited for Arctic conditions: cold weather gear, ice-capable vessels (incl. icebreakers), long-range surveillance,

   naval / air assets able to operate in polar climates.

   * Ensure a more balanced burden-sharing within NATO to reduce reliance on the US

   for defence.

   * Establish a clearer, unified, regional command or coordination mechanism within

   NATO for the Arctic theatre (while respecting national sovereignty).

3. Balanced Burden-Sharing within NATO

* European NATO states are expected to increase their defence spending, particularly for an Arctic/Northern posture, not just in aggregate, but also for

  targeted capabilities.

  * Coordinated procurement and joint development of infrastructure, logistics, and

  systems for the High North to avoid duplication and reduce cost.

  * Transparent contribution reporting and mutual accountability.

4. Nordic & Arctic Regional Cooperation under NATO & EU Frameworks

   * Reinforce cooperation among European & Arctic states in joint exercises, intelligence sharing, infrastructure, in NATO, NORDEFCO and EU contexts.

   * Engage with local/regional authorities/communities (including indigenous populations) in planning and oversight where territory/sovereignty / local impact are involved.  
   * Strengthen the work carried out by NATO countries within the Arctic Council.

   * Enhance NORDEFCOcooperation in parallel with NATO collaboration.

   82. ## **A Continent of Opportunities: A Liberal Strategy for Development Cooperation with Africa**

### ***Passed Autumn 2025***

Submitted by: Junge Liberale

Co-Signed by: JOVD, LLY, Venstres Ungdom, LHG, JNC, Alliance Youth, JL, Nowoczesna

Youth, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz Youth, JUNOS  
Considering that:

* Development cooperation is an important part of the European CFSP.

  Providing

  support to developing countries in key areas has been a high priority to date,

  and it is important that this remains the case.

* Development cooperation has recently often been portrayed negatively in the

  media.

* Time and again, we get the impression that the financial resources provided under the umbrella of development cooperation to support states with weak  
  infrastructure and supply situations are not being used wisely.

* Well-organized and realistic development cooperation can provide significant

  support to structurally weak regions and countries that are often ravaged by

  multiple crises, such as local conflicts or climate change.

* With the growing strategic considerations of many developing and emerging countries between turning to the West or to authoritarian states such as Russia

  and China, this presents a key opportunity for economic partnerships.

* As part of the Belt and Road Initiative, China is gaining influence worldwide by providing funds for infrastructure projects such as bridges, ports, railways, and dams.  
* The goal of China is to create political dependence through diverse interdependencies. Approximately 150 countries worldwide have joined the Belt

  and Road Initiative, including Austria, Italy, Portugal, and most countries on the African continent.

* Western development cooperation has failed to achieve clear deliverables in several decades. This has resulted in countless missed opportunities to work with partners such as in North Africa to increase prosperity in all participating countries and strengthen democratic institutions.  
* Industrialized countries bear a significant share of the responsibility for the tangible effects of climate change in Africa.  
* The North African countries are primarily transit countries for refugees from sub-Sahara Africa.

* The spread of jihadist movements across parts of Africa reflects deep governance

  challenges, instability, and socioeconomic disparities that fuel radicalization and threaten both regional and European security.

Believing that:

* Development cooperation must focus primarily on the transfer of know-how and

  innovation, rather than on one-off financial contributions that do not offer structural and therefore long-term solutions.

* Development cooperation should be brought more into the public eye, but it should also become more transparent in its own right, so that populist narratives and misinformation seeking to delegitimize ODA in general have less  
  fertile ground to grow.

* The EU's development cooperation must be aligned with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

* It is crucial that the feasibility of these goals for developing countries is carefully examined at the multilateral level. In addition to environmental considerations, social and economic aspects must also be given

appropriate

consideration and carefully weighed up.

* Security cooperation is a fundamental pillar for Africa’s sustainable development, as stability and peace are prerequisites for economic growth,

  investment, freedom, democracy, and effective governance.

Emphasizing that:

* Projects must generally be planned thoroughly and for the long term, implemented

  with as little bureaucracy as possible, and their impact adequately monitored.

  It must also be clearly stated and factored into the budget that development aid

  is intended to alleviate the causes of migration, thereby reducing the number of

  people seeking refuge in Europe.

* In order to improve the image of development cooperation in society in the short  
  and long term, no money should be invested in projects that give the impression  
  of squandering financial resources.  
* Of the five North African countries—Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Tunisia, and Egypt—none are rated as stable by the Fragile State Index. Should these countries collapse, this would mean great suffering for the local population, a  
  loss of prosperity, the loss of a trading partner, and streams of refugees heading for Europe. The most important goal of development cooperation must  
  therefore be to stabilize countries and prevent them from failing. Efforts that go beyond stabilization must serve to promote democracy in partner countries.  
* The maintenance of inhumane detention camps, through which the EU shifts its  
  responsibility to areas not covered by its Convention on Human Rights, must be  
  stopped.

LYMEC calls for:

* Advocating for the targeted promotion of civil society organizations, local initiatives, and trustworthy partners in autocratically governed states, provided that this can be done transparently and in compliance with human rights  
  standards. Direct government payments should be ruled out in these cases.

* A clear distinction between non-repayable development aid in the form of financial assistance and loans that are to be repaid. A distinction should be made between the following two categories:

Category A: Know-how or expenditure only for essential structural improvements, such

as in the areas of health, food, and drinking water infrastructure, as well as for corresponding disaster relief efforts. The repayment of expenses is determined by contracts on a case-by-case basis. Climate protection projects may also fall under Category A in cases of particular urgency.

Category B: Financial support for non-essential structural improvements. This should include loans that are generally repayable with interest.

* Advocating for the close monitoring of projects in countries where corruption, authoritarian rule, or massive human rights violations exist. Projects with a proven impact on civil society—especially for women, minorities, and LGBTQ

  individuals—should remain possible, even if government conditions are difficult.

  Projects involving government actors must be suspended if cooperation in compliance with human rights standards is not possible.

* The deepening of the CFSP in the European Union by pooling national development  
  cooperation measures at EU level in the long term, thereby saving costs by eliminating duplicate structures.  
* A serious European connectivity strategy on the African continent.  
* Focusing European development cooperation with African countries and the African  
  Union on sustainable job creation and knowledge transfer for the African population, as well as infrastructure development and new digital and climate  
  projects.  
* Increased cooperation between Western and African countries to remove barriers  
  to market entry in order to facilitate private investment in African countries. To this end, we want to expand and supplement existing free trade agreements  
  with the aim of establishing multilateral free trade agreements that enable the  
  free movement of goods and labor.

* Western countries to work together with their African partners to reduce bureaucracy, simplify visa procedures, make it easier to raise capital, and set

  up targeted support and advisory programs for companies wishing to invest in

  Africa.

* Using our relationships and resources to promote effective local solutions, since the ability of individual actors to take sufficient environmental and climate action is at times limited.

* Supporting African delegations in climate negotiations on a partnership basis.

* Using targeted support measures to promote the rapid expansion of solar power  
  plants in the Sahara in all North African countries. The goal should be to produce climate-neutral hydrogen locally that can also be used to power European  
  industry.

* Supporting our partners in creating humane refugee accommodation where asylum

  applications to the European Union can be submitted directly.

* Concluding migration agreements between the European Union and North African

  countries, to stop human trafficking and illegal migration directly on the coasts of North Africa.

* Strengthening cooperation with African partners in intelligence sharing, training, and development support to more effectively combat jihadism and

  address the root causes of violent islamic extremism.

* European development cooperation should place a particular focus on partner  
  countries that maintain effective cooperation on migration management and

  readmission of rejected ayslum seekers.

  83. ## **Lost in Time and Lost in Space? Europe’s Wake-Up Call for Space Security and Sovereignty\!**

### ***Passed Spring 2026***

Submitted by: Junge Liberale \- JuLis

Co-Signed by: ZeMolodizhka, Jongliberalen, Venstres Ungdom, Young Green Liberals  
   
Switzerland, JOVD, Jeunes MR, Lithuanian Liberal Youth, JUNOS, Nowoczesna Youth, Attistibai Youth, LHG, Joventut Nacionalista Catalunya, Mladih Naša Stranka, LDLU, ERPY, USR Tineret, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

LYMEC notes that:

* Space systems underpin Europe’s economy and security and are increasingly targeted by jamming, cyberattacks, and counterspace capabilities.  
* Europe’s access-to-space is strategically constrained by a very low orbital launch cadence compared to the US and China weakening resilience, learning curves, and competitiveness.  
* Orbital congestion and debris are a systemic security risk; destructive actions in orbit can create long-lived debris that endangers all operators and services.  
* International law already sets a clear red line against nuclear weapons / weapons of mass destruction in space.  
* Global consensus-building is active but fragile: the UN general assembly has called for ending destructive direct-ascent anti-satellite missile tests, and recent UN-level diplomacy shows how contested enforcement and verification remain.  
* The “race to the Moon” is accelerating into an infrastructure-and-standards contest with competing blocs seeking partners and influence.  
* Europe has credible building blocks for lunar autonomy and a lunar economy, yet political mandate and sustained funding determine speed and scale.  
* The EU is pursuing a sovereign connectivity constellation to provide secure communications and broadband services \- an important step for strategic autonomy if it is implemented competitively and at scale.

LYMEC believes that:

* A war in space would be catastrophic for everyone \- especially highly digitized societies.  
* The nuclear taboo in orbit must be strengthened with credible norms, transparency, and verification pathways.  
* Space security must combine rules-based governance with resilience  
* Europe’s strategic autonomy requires: reliable, affordable launch capacity at high cadence, open, easy-to-use connectivity and data infrastructure, and a regulatory environment that enables NewSpace to scale across Europe.  
* The Moon should not become a sphere of coercion or exclusion. Resource utilisation should be governed so that it is peaceful, transparent, and compatible with the Outer Space Treaty.  
* The lunar economy could benefit from commercial space flight. US companies like SpaceX, Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic currently dominate the sector with reusable rockets, satellite services and space tourism. It offers great opportunities for research and engineering, with an income stream of individual tickets that run into the millions.  
* For speed and scale, commercial space flights can create a needed influx of funds.  
* The EU should lead a coalition of responsible “space countries” to protect the orbital environment against destabilizing actors and incentives  
* A flagship international science project can be a stabilizer and confidence-building instrument, provided it is paired with hard security measures and clear participation conditions.

LYMEC calls for:

1) Preventing war in space  
* Champion an EU-led “Keep Space Peaceful & Usable” agenda  
* Make the ban on Weapons of Mass Destruction in orbit a politically enforceable red line. The EU needs to push for verification concepts, transparency measures, and coordinated consequences for violations.  
* Turn the UN general assembly call to end destructive anti-satellite testing into a wider binding norm.


2\) Increasing Europe’s launch cadence and autonomy

* A European “Cadence First” industrial plan: scale launch production, streamline range operations, enable rapid licensing, and procure launch services in a way that rewards reliability and flight rate (not only legacy structures).  
* Consider commercial space flight as a source to fund an increased European launch cadence and autonomy.  
* Establish EU-level rapid reconstitution capability (launch \+ satellite buses \+ terminals) for crisis replacement of critical services.

3\) Modernizing and speeding up ESA

* Reform ESA procurement and program governance to increase tempo: more milestone-based contracting, and clearer prioritization toward infrastructure platforms that unlock markets.  
* Back a clear political mandate and budget line for Europe’s launch to the Moon via ESA capabilities.  
* Make full participation in European space capability-building the default: support pathways for every EU country to engage meaningfully with ESA programs and European space industrial bases. EU funding needs to be aligned to incentivize reduced fragmentation.

4\) A credible European Moon \- Mars pathway

* Commit to “Europe on the Moon” infrastructure: support the Moonlight programme as a European anchor in lunar comms/nav services and interoperability with allied standards.  
* Build a European position on lunar resources to support lawful, transparent resource utilisation under clear governance, aligned with free access and due regard principles.  
* Keep Mars as a long-term objective: expand international cooperation for deep-space tech and habitation research, with Europe owning critical enabling layers.

5\) Space traffic management and debris as security policy

* Advance EU-wide space traffic management (STM) and resilience rules, aligned with the EU approach to STM and the EU’s security/defence space strategy.  
* Establishing a Space Debris Trade System (SDTS), whereby a pollution permit will be required for every kilogramme of waste in space. In order to limit space debris, a maximum permissible level of space littering should be set. This cap must be based on what scientists and engineers consider to be the maximum permissible amount for a still controllable risk of collisions with debris. The SDTS certificate must be available at the time of satellite launch in order to cover the potential debris at all times. When space debris is removed, new certificates for the debris remover are created in the same amount.

6\) Growing a European NewSpace ecosystem

* Push for national and European legal clarity for private space activity so startups can scale and invest with confidence.  
* Expand European space startup funding and procurement pathways to increase competition, innovation, and security of supply.  
* Pursue an ISS-like new multinational space station framework as a confidence-building, scientific, and industrial project among major spacefaring democracies.  
* Implement a performant IRIS² with startup-grade accessibility: standardized interfaces, transparent pricing, simple onboarding/procurement, and open service models so that SMEs and startups can build on it easily.  
* Establishing a network of Competence Hubs throughout the EU with simplified tax regimes. NewSpace founders should be able to set up their businesses easily and without red tape and be exempted from bureaucratic obligations as far as possible.

  84. ## **Defending Greenland’s Sovereignty: A Liberal European Response to Modern Imperialism**

### ***Passed Spring 2026*** 

Submitted by: Radikal Ungdom, Venstres Ungdom, Junge Liberale \- JuLis, Young Greenliberals

Co-Signed by: Finnish Centre Youth, Finnish Centre Students, ZeMolodizhka, Jeunes MR, Centerpartiets Ungdomsförbund, JUNOS, Nowoczesna Youth, Lithuanian Liberal Youth, PSG Mladi, Attistibai Youth, LHG, EYU, Joventut Nacionalista Catalunya, Young LIberals (UK), Mladih Naša Stranka, ERPY, Mladih Naša Stranka, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

Remembering That

* Greenland has been an official part of the Kingdom of Denmark since 1814, following the Treaty of Kiel.  
*  As the former colonial power in Greenland, Denmark's historical role continues to shape the relationship between the two countries and forms part of the backdrop for ongoing Greenlandic aspirations for greater self-determination.  
* Greenland achieved expanded self-governance in 2009, granting its government authority over domestic affairs while Denmark retains responsibility for foreign affairs, defence, and monetary policy.  
* Denmark and the United States are longstanding allies, and have worked together on defence and security for decades, including the 1951 Defence Agreement governing the American military presence in Greenland.  
* Greenland is not a member of the European Union, while Denmark is a full EU member state.  
* Greenland, as an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, falls under NATO’s collective defence framework.

Noting That 

* A majority of Greenlanders, and all political parties in Greenland have expressed a desire for independence as a long term goal, and that the decision of independence is a greenlandic prerogative.   
* Economic development is a precondition for a functioning Greenland, independent of the Danish block grant. In this context, Greenland’s natural resources are becoming increasingly important for economic resilience, industrial policy, and strategic autonomy.  
* U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire and intention to acquire Greenland one way or another, citing national security interests, while Greenlandic and Danish leaders have rejected any notion that the territory is for sale.  
* The Arctic is of growing strategic importance due to its role in military positioning, maritime routes, space-related infrastructure, critical raw materials, and broader great-power competition.  
* There has been an US military presence in Greenland since 1941, which was of significant strategic importance for Europe throughout the Cold War.  
* Authoritarian powers, like Russia and the People´s Republic of China (PRC) have  articulated a strategic interest in the Arctic and more specifically Greenland and Svalbard.

Believing That 

* The right to self-determination is a fundamental liberal principle, and the Greenlandic people must be allowed to determine their own future without coercion from any foreign power.  
* Any change in Greenland's political status must be driven exclusively by the democratic will of the Greenlandic people.  
* The aggressive rhetoric used by the United States with respect to Greenland is a breach of the principles of rule-based order.  
* Arctic security must be based on cooperation, rules-based order, democratic alliances, and respect for sovereignty, rather than territorial expansion, coercion, and great-power pressure.  
* Greenland’s geopolitical importance extends far beyond the question of formal sovereignty: the Arctic is increasingly central to European and transatlantic security.  
* In a time of increasing competition over critical raw materials, shipping routes, and strategic infrastructure, Europe must not leave Arctic policy to unilateral action by outside powers, but must develop a coherent and responsible approach that combines security, sustainability, and respect for the rights of Greenlanders.

 

LYMEC Calls For

* Institutional investors, such as the European Investment Fund and the European Investment Bank, to invest in Greenland, with the aim of supporting its economic sustainability and greater economic independence away from the Danish bloc grant.  
* National governments and European institutions to unequivocally condemn any military or economic threats against Greenland's territorial integrity, and be ready to back this up with concrete actions if necessary.   
* The United States to respect the democratic and sovereign rights of Greenland.  
* For the European Union to actively promote Greenland's potential route toward membership of the European Union, if the people of Greenland so choose.   
* The Danish government to acknowledge and take steps to rectify the injustices of Danish colonialism in Greenland.  
* The European Union to strengthen its strategic commitment in the Arctic through greater investment in security, infrastructure, research, and diplomatic presence, in order to reduce reliance on unilateral action by outside powers and to contribute to regional stability.  
* The European Union and its member states to support fair, sustainable, and locally beneficial development of Greenland’s natural resources, in ways that strengthen Greenland’s economic self-determination and reduce European dependencies on authoritarian or non-European suppliers.  
* A European military presence on Greenland, which complements the strategic value of Pittufik Space Base, and which safeguards European strategic interests in the Arctic against infringements from authoritarian adversaries such as Russia and the PRC.

  85. ## **Guaranteeing peace and freedom on our continent: Towards a Credible European Nuclear Deterrent**

### ***Passed Spring 2026***

Submitted by: Junge liberale NEOS (Austria)

Co-signed by: Jóvenes de Ciudadanos (Spain), Jongliberalen (Belgium), Jungfreisinnige Schweiz (Switzerland), Young Green Liberals (Switzerland), ZeMolodizhka (Ukraine), Mladi hrvatski liberali (Croatia), Venstres Ungdom (Denmark), Momentum TizenX (Hungary), PSG Mladi (Serbia), Junge Liberale \- JuLis (Germany), JOVD (The Netherlands), Youth forum of Naša stranka (Bosnia and Herzegovina), Liberale Hochschulgruppen (Germany), Jonge Democraten (The Netherlands)

Noting that:

* Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has fundamentally altered the European security environment and demonstrated the continued relevance of nuclear deterrence in global geopolitics.  
* The Russian Federation continues to maintain and modernise one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals while repeatedly using nuclear threats as a tool of coercion against European democracies.  
* The security architecture of Europe has long relied on the nuclear umbrella of the United States through NATO, which has been essential in maintaining peace and deterrence on the continent.  
* Growing geopolitical instability and increasing uncertainty regarding the long-term reliability of U.S. security guarantees highlight the need for Europe to strengthen its strategic autonomy within the transatlantic alliance.  
* That France and the United Kingdom, the only two European nuclear powers, have recognized a European dimension to their deterrence strategies in the Northwood declaration.  
* France is currently the only nuclear-armed member of the European Union and has indicated in its forward deterrence doctrine its willingness to open cooperation and coordination on nuclear deterrence with European partners.  
* European defence cooperation has intensified in recent years, including initiatives aimed at strengthening joint defence capabilities and strategic coordination within the European Union.  
* The UK and several member states have already signaled their interest in participating in France’s forward deterrence.

Acknowledging that:

* Nuclear weapons represent a grave humanitarian risk and the long-term objective of liberal security policy must remain global nuclear disarmament.  
* However, as long as authoritarian powers such as Russia and People's Republic of China maintain nuclear arsenals and use nuclear threats to destabilise democratic societies, credible deterrence remains a necessary component of European security.

Believing that:

* The protection of liberal democracy, human rights, and European sovereignty requires credible and effective deterrence against nuclear coercion and aggression.  
* That while short of being a true nuclear umbrella, France’s forward deterrence is an important step towards EU strategic autonomy aggression.  
* The European Union with its own foreign and security policy needs an European armed force.  
* A European framework for nuclear deterrence would reduce strategic dependency, increase collective resilience, and ensure that decisions affecting European security are made with democratic accountability.  
* Shared responsibility among European states would provide greater stability and reliability than reliance on a single national nuclear deterrent.  
* Democratic oversight, transparency, and civilian control are essential elements of any European security architecture.

LYMEC calls for:

* The governments of European Union Member States and democratic partners on the continent to begin structured discussions on the development of a European nuclear deterrence framework within the broader context of European defence integration, with the goal being joint European Armed Forces.  
* The European Union and its Member States to invest in nuclear research and technological development, including civilian nuclear energy and relevant dual-use capabilities, in order to reinforce Europe’s strategic resilience, maintain technological expertise, and support a credible and autonomous security architecture.  
* The command structure must be clearly defined and democratically legitimate. It must moreover be pan-European in nature and must not be under the control of individual Member States. However, until this can be achieved, individual Member States should also be able to proceed in accordance with Article 46 of the EU Treaty and bring French nuclear weapons under joint controlThis should, of course, only take place with the consent of the countries that provide the nuclear weapons \- nuclear weapons from France, for example, should not be able to be placed under joint control against their will by a qualified majority.  
* France to initiate consultations with European partners on extending its nuclear deterrence as a temporary European nuclear umbrella while a broader European framework is developed.  
* The European Union and willing Member and Partner States to explore mechanisms for shared financial, strategic, and operational responsibility for nuclear deterrence in Europe.  
* The development, in the long term, of a European defence structure in which nuclear deterrence responsibilities are embedded within a future European defence union or European army under democratic European command and oversight. This shall also include the development of a strategic submarine fleet to ensure a second-strike capability.  
* The European Parliament to be involved in shaping democratic accountability mechanisms for European-level security and deterrence policies.  
* The European Union and its Member States to continue pursuing international nuclear arms control and disarmament efforts while ensuring that Europe maintains a credible deterrent as long as nuclear threats persist.
